title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
A music AI generator was trained on copyrighted songs scraped from the internet without permission. The system was deployed to users who could generate music that reproduced sections of recognizable songs when given prompts describing the original work. This failure happened at the training stage, where the company did not obtain authorization for the material it used to build the model, and at deployment, where no guard against reproducing copyrighted works was implemented.

The failure was one of training data governance. The company admits it was trained on essentially all music files available online, obtained through scraping YouTube, Deezer, and other sources. No authorization check happened before this data entered the system, and no mechanism prevented the deployed generator from producing outputs that mimicked specific copyrighted songs when users requested them. A human review of training data sources and licensing status, conducted before deployment, would have surfaced the unauthorized use.

It is not established whether the reproduction of copyrighted material was intentional, whether the system was designed to mimic specific works, or what the ultimate legal outcome will be. The lawsuits and settlements reported show only that courts and companies have found the training practices indefensible.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, and others have filed lawsuits against AI music generators Udio and Suno, claiming the companies scraped thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their systems. The labels allege that both companies not only used massive amounts of music illegally but also directly reproduce sections of famous songs in their generated outputs. The record labels submitted a lengthy list of affected artists, ranging from The Beatles and Frank Sinatra to contemporary performers like Coldplay and Future, totaling thousands of copyrighted works they claim were used without authorization.

To support their claims, the record labels demonstrated they could recreate versions of famous songs by using specific prompts describing musical characteristics like decade, genre, and artist style. For example, they generated a song mimicking Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You" and another copying Green Day's "American Idiot" lyrics and melody. The companies have refused to disclose their training data but previously claimed their use qualifies as fair use. Udio was sued in New York while Suno faced legal action in Massachusetts, with the lawsuits setting up a significant court battle over generative AI and copyright protections.
